readingCallout.label: How to read this section
readingCallout.text: Layer 1 (suppliers) and Layer 3 (PlayBlue's actual layer) are not comparable on revenue — different margin structures, different jobs. The only chart below that is a fair apples-to-apples comparison is the Layer 2/3 retail-revenue chart in 5b. Everything else is shown as context, labelled as such.

suppliersCallout.label: The point of this chart
suppliersCallout.text: This is supplier-pool sizing, not a leaderboard PlayBlue is trying to climb. Puma outselling Adidas and Nike in India, by localising hard on price and celebrity endorsement, is a signal about _Indian consumer behaviour toward global brands_ — useful context for what PlayBlue's assortment mix and price ladder should look like — but it says nothing about whether curated multi-brand retail works here. That question is answered in Layer 3, which is empty.

retailCallout.label: What this chart actually says
retailCallout.text: PlayBlue's five-year ambition is 21% larger than Decathlon India's current business, built over sixteen years with a €100M programme behind it — and Decathlon captures full margin where PlayBlue would capture retail margin only on comparable revenue. The ₹100 Cr phase-one target is a more honest comparator: roughly a quarter of Technosport's current revenue, achievable, and the right number to be judged on in the near term.

layers.title: Layer 1 · Nike, Adidas, Puma, Asics, Yonex — suppliers
layers.desc: Sell wholesale to retailers including, potentially, PlayBlue. Compete only through their own flagship stores.

body.label: Position
body.text: Puma leads India at ₹3,274 Cr (CY2024, up 10%) with 570+ stores, having overtaken Adidas in 2021 by localising hard — cricket sponsorships, Bollywood ambassadors, mass-market pricing. Only about a quarter of Puma's India revenue is sports performance; the rest is lifestyle and athleisure. Adidas sits at roughly ₹3,114 Cr, pushing its Indian national cricket team association. Nike, the world's largest sportswear brand, is fourth in India at ₹1,380 Cr, up 16%, having scaled back store count while retaining brand equity.

body.label: Relationship to PlayBlue
body.text: Suppliers, and only channel-competitors where they run their own D2C stores — a narrow overlap, not a scale contest. Their India revenue is context for assortment planning (who to prioritise, what commercial terms are realistic) not a target to outgrow. Note what Puma's lead does say: in India, localisation and price accessibility beat pure global brand equity — worth carrying into how PlayBlue prices its own curation.

layers.title: Layer 2 · Decathlon — vertically integrated, legally single-brand
layers.desc: ₹4,133 Cr FY25 · ~130 stores · the price anchor and the format benchmark

body.label: Position
body.text: India's largest sports retail player. Big-box format, ~20 in-house brands it owns outright, aggressive pricing — a functional dry-fit t-shirt at ₹399. Returned to profitability in FY24 with ₹197 Cr net profit on ₹4,008 Cr revenue.

body.label: Trajectory
body.text: €100M committed over five years. Expanding from ~110–132 to 190 stores across 90+ cities, targeting ~₹8,000 Cr by 2030. ~68% locally sourced in 2024, targeting 85% by 2026. Distributes through Ajio as well as own channels — and has reportedly petitioned the Indian government for multi-brand status so it can stock rival products such as Adidas and Garmin, confirming it currently cannot.

body.label: Why the model matters more than the number
body.text: Decathlon owns its brands, so it captures manufacturer margin plus retail margin, and its FDI classification as single-brand is a direct consequence of that structure. It sets the price anchor and format expectation PlayBlue must argue against, but it is not a like-for-like business-model comparator — it is the model PlayBlue is _not_ running.

layers.title: Layer 2 · Technosport and BlissClub — the vertically integrated challengers
layers.desc: ₹436 Cr and ~₹250 Cr ARR, both growing fast · absent from PlayBlue's stated competitive framing

body.label: Technosport
body.text: Founded 2015 in Bengaluru. ₹436 Cr FY25, targeting ₹600 Cr FY26. Raised ₹175 Cr from A91 Partners. Controls its own manufacturing and fabric technology — moisture-wicking, anti-microbial, UV protection — selling performance wear at entry-level prices, effectively Decathlon's playbook run by a startup. 300 new stores announced on ₹200 Cr, directly contesting the same scarce retail space PlayBlue needs.

body.label: BlissClub
body.text: Founded 2020, women-first. Started with a single product — leggings designed for Indian women. ₹92 Cr FY24 to a ₹250 Cr annualised run rate by January 2026. Raised over $21M from Elevation Capital and Eight Roads, raising a further $25M.

body.label: Why they belong in this analysis
body.text: Structurally the same layer as Decathlon — own product, own manufacturing, own retail — not Layer 3 peers of PlayBlue. But they are proof, right now, that owning product and price beats curating other brands, at least so far in India. Their absence from PlayBlue's own competitive framing is a real gap, not because they compete unit-for-unit but because they are evidence against the Layer 3 thesis.

layers.title: Layer 3 · Multi-brand curated retail — PlayBlue's actual layer, and it is nearly empty
layers.desc: No dedicated multi-brand sports chain occupies this space at scale in India today

body.label: What exists
body.text: General multi-brand fashion retailers (Shoppers Stop, Lifestyle) carry sports and athleisure sections but are not sport-specialist. Reliance Retail has been reported since mid-2024 to be exploring a Decathlon-rival format and to be seeking multi-brand retail permission from the government for exactly this purpose — the same regulatory question in finding G. No confirmed launch as of this brief; the most visible recent Reliance sports-adjacent move is Yousta's licensed FIFA apparel line, which is fashion merchandise rather than curated multi-brand sports retail.

body.label: Why this layer deserves particular attention
body.text: An unoccupied layer supports two distinct readings: either no operator has executed multi-brand sports curation well in India yet, or the model faces structural headwinds here — FDI considerations around genuine multi-brand structures, and Layer 2 operators matching price without sacrificing curation credibility. Reliance's reported interest in this same space, backed by considerably greater capital, is a relevant data point for either reading and worth surfacing directly.

layers.title: Layer 4 · Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, Ajio — marketplaces
layers.desc: Aggregate many brands like PlayBlue does, but as a commission platform, not an inventory-owning curator

body.label: Position
body.text: Horizontal and fashion-led marketplaces carrying the widest sports assortment with the fastest national fulfilment. Online sports apparel demand on these platforms grew over 35% year on year in 2024. Ajio carries Decathlon. India's online fashion order volume rose more than 20.9% in FY24.

body.label: Relationship to PlayBlue
body.text: Structurally the nearest thing to "multi-brand" that exists at scale in India — but as a platform taking commission on third-party inventory, not a curator taking ownership and margin risk the way PlayBlue's stores would. They set the consumer's baseline expectation on price, selection and delivery speed, which is exactly what the 4-hour promise will be benchmarked against.

layers.title: Layer 5 · Unorganised and counterfeit retail — the real incumbent
layers.desc: Price-led, dominant outside metros, the actual base PlayBlue is converting from

body.label: Position
body.text: Unorganised and counterfeit retail continues to dominate large parts of the category. Buyers in tier-II and tier-III cities substantially prefer low-cost alternatives, and imitation jerseys, gym wear and athleisure are widely available at a fraction of branded prices.

body.label: Why it matters more than its place in the list suggests
body.text: PlayBlue is not primarily fighting Decathlon for share — it is trying to convert unorganised demand into organised demand at a materially higher price point. That is a slower, harder conversion than a share war between organised players, and it makes price perception the decisive variable.
